Why not
- “Gross margin” (revenue less cost of goods sold, divided by revenue) assumes a separable COGS tied to producing physical goods. Banks don’t sell goods — they intermediate funds and provide financial services — so there’s no analogous, consistently reported COGS line.  
- Bank revenue is split into net interest income (interest earned less interest paid) and noninterest income (fees, trading, investment banking, asset management, etc.). What professional investors and analysts use instead (and why)
- Net interest margin (NIM): net interest income divided by average interest-earning assets. Shows how well the bank is earning from lending/asset investment relative to funding. Sensitive to interest-rate moves and deposit behavior, so it can change materially year to year (more than 2% of the metric in many cases).
- Efficiency ratio: noninterest expense divided by total revenue. A measure of the bank’s operating leverage/expense control. Movements of a few percentage points are common and meaningful.
- Return on equity (ROE) and return on assets (ROA): overall profitability measures that can swing with revenue mix, credit performance, capital levels and market-driven trading income.
- Pre-provision operating profit and provision for credit losses: show core earnings and credit-cost volatility (loan losses) which can materially affect net results.
- Revenue composition (net interest income vs. noninterest income): noninterest income — especially trading and investment banking — can be very volatile from year to year.

How volatility compares to “±2%”
- Because banks’ revenue mix and interest-rate sensitivity can cause sizable swings in NIM, trading revenues, provisions and efficiency, these metrics commonly move by more than “roughly 2%” year-to-year. Market-sensitive items (CIB trading, underwriting) in particular can change a lot in a single year. Therefore you should expect greater variability than the ~2% threshold you cited.
